Paragraph: By slaying an ascetic, I committed a crime that no man should ever have. Alone, shattered by a disaster, beyond description and afraid of its consequences, I stood stunned. Finally taking some water I wended my way to the cottage where I beheld an old couple, who were blind. With none to help them they were like birds, whose wings had been severed. They sat talking of their son not knowing he would no more fetch them water, for a fault of mine. My grief doubled at the thought, hearing my footsteps, the old father said, 'Why the delay my son? Your mother waits for you impatiently. Give us the water. To us who are blind you are our eyes and our very life. We have no other refuge other than you. Speak my child, why are you silent?' As I looked at him my heart filled with dread, my voice felt strangled and my words came garbled, but I managed to say, 'I am a Kshatriya, Dasaratha is my name. I am not your son but the cause of a great calamity. Noble sire, as I stood on the banks of the Sarayu I shot an arrow at what I thought was an elephant. To my horror, I soon found out, that my arrow had not struck an elephant but had fatally wounded your son.'
Characters_Involved: The blind old father of the ascetic
The blind old mother of the ascetic
Situation/Problem_Faced: Dasaratha, having accidentally killed the ascetic, is now burdened with the task of informing the ascetic's blind and dependent parents. He faces intense guilt and fear of the consequences, experiencing a doubling of his grief upon seeing their vulnerability and hearing their innocent longing for their deceased son. The emotional and physical paralysis he feels makes delivering the devastating news incredibly difficult.
Key_Teaching/Action_Taken: This passage vividly illustrates the profound psychological torment of carrying an 'unpardonable crime' and being forced to confront its direct victims. Dasaratha's inability to speak clearly and his 'strangled' voice reflect the immense internal conflict and distress. His forced confession highlights the weight of his actions and the devastating impact of his truth, which shatters the old couple's world.
Outcome/Resolution: Dasaratha finally confesses his role in their son's death to the blind parents. This act of confession, while necessary, unleashes immense grief and despair upon the innocent old couple, further solidifying Dasaratha's 'unpardonable sin' in his own mind.

Spiritual_Psychological_Concept_Indian.Concept: Papa (The 'crime' or sin committed, which Dasaratha deeply internalizes and acknowledges.)
Karma Phala (The direct consequence of his 'fault,' which he is now forced to deliver to the innocent parents, leading to their suffering.)
Dukha (The pervasive suffering of all characters in this scene: Dasaratha's torment, and the immense grief that will soon befall the blind parents.)
Brahmahatya (The potential sin of killing a Brahmin, which was averted by the ascetic's caste revelation, but the burden of killing an innocent remains.)
Viyoga-Dukha (The impending suffering of the blind parents due to the separation from their only son, a direct result of Dasaratha's action.)

Brief_Summary_Spiritual: Dasaratha confronts the direct manifestation of his 'Papa' (sin) and the Karma Phala of his actions by facing the ascetic's blind parents. His profound guilt and Dukha (suffering) are intensified as he witnesses their innocence and dependence. The harrowing task of revealing their son's death, which will plunge them into 'Viyoga-Dukha,' solidifies his internal burden, underscoring the deep spiritual and moral ramifications of his 'unpardonable crime.'
Brief_Summary_Psychological: Psychologically, Dasaratha is in an extreme state of guilt and self-blame, bordering on emotional paralysis. His grief doubles as he witnesses the tragic vulnerability of the ascetic's blind parents, leading to overwhelming anxiety and dread about delivering the devastating news. His struggle to speak—'voice felt strangled and my words came garbled'—illustrates the immense psychological burden of being the bearer of such calamity. This entire sequence portrays the profound trauma of directly confronting the victims of one's unintentional but fatal error, cementing an indelible sense of responsibility and sorrow.
